title: Riverbend Community Bank — Ransomware on the Wire-Transfer Workstation
summary: An out-of-hours ransomware exercise for a mid-market US community bank. The exercise covers initial detection, escalation, containment, regulator notification, and recovery decisions over an 8-hour window.
setting: You are the on-call SecOps Lead at Riverbend Community Bank, a $1.8B-asset community bank in upstate New York with 12 branches and roughly 220 employees. The bank uses Microsoft 365, a SentinelOne EDR rollout (90% coverage), Splunk Cloud SIEM, and a managed-SOC contract with a regional MSSP. You are subject to NYDFS Cybersecurity Regulation (23 NYCRR 500) and FFIEC IT examination. It is 02:14 on a Tuesday.
facilitator_notes: Pace: 6 to 10 minutes per scene. Allow disagreement on decisions before recording the chosen option. After-action discussion should focus on decisions where the team split.

scenes.narrative: Your PagerDuty fires. The MSSP has flagged a SentinelOne detection on WS-OPS-04, the workstation in the wire-transfer office: 17,000 file modifications in 60 seconds, all writing the extension `.lockbear`. The on-call MSSP analyst has automatically isolated the host. The wire-transfer team starts at 06:30. You have not seen detections like this from this MSSP before.

options.label: Acknowledge the page and decide to investigate after the team comes in at 06:30.
options.consequence: By 04:00 the same indicator triggers on three more workstations. You wake up to a much bigger incident.

options.label: Open Splunk, confirm the detection on WS-OPS-04, and start scoping which other endpoints have touched the same indicator.
options.consequence: You confirm the detection and find one neighbouring workstation talking to the same C2 IP in the last hour. You now have scope.

options.label: Tell the MSSP to re-image WS-OPS-04 immediately and go back to sleep.
options.consequence: The MSSP destroys the only forensic evidence. Three hours later another host fires, and the regulator will later ask why you destroyed the artefact.

scenes.narrative: It is now 02:35. You have one isolated workstation (WS-OPS-04) and one suspicious neighbour (WS-OPS-02). The MSSP analyst is on the bridge. The on-call CISO is sleeping. Wire-transfer cutoff windows open at 06:30; the bank typically clears $40M of wires before 09:00.

options.label: Wake the CISO and the COO. Open the Incident Response Plan binder.
options.consequence: The CISO joins the bridge in 12 minutes. She agrees to escalate per the IR Plan and asks you to prepare a draft notification for NYDFS.

options.label: Handle it yourself with the MSSP — no need to wake the executives over a single isolated host.
options.consequence: By 04:30 you are running the response solo. The COO finds out from a Slack message at 06:15 and is furious that wire transfers are paused without his knowledge.

options.label: Call the FBI Cyber Division and the FS-ISAC right now.
options.consequence: FS-ISAC takes a report. The FBI agent on duty notes the case but says they cannot meaningfully help in the first hour. You have used 25 minutes you could have spent containing.

scenes.narrative: By 04:10 SentinelOne has fired on four hosts. One is the file server FS-CORE-01, which holds the loan-origination scans. Wire-transfer staff arrive in 140 minutes. The MSSP escalates to their Tier-3 lead and asks you for authority to take broader action.

options.label: Authorise containment: isolate every host with the indicator and disable the suspected service account.
options.consequence: Containment holds. You have lost three hours but you have stopped the spread. Wire transfers will be delayed; the COO will need to be told before market open.

options.label: Wait for daylight and the CISO before authorising anything beyond the isolation already done.
options.consequence: By 06:00 the file server is fully encrypted and the actor has staged 8GB of data to a Mega.nz account. This is now a data-exfiltration incident, not just ransomware.

scenes.narrative: It is 03:30. Containment is in place. The CISO is on the bridge. You have the chosen extension (`.lockbear`), one C2 IP, and a service account (`svc-backup`) that authenticated to four hosts via WinRM in the last 12 hours.

decision.prompt: Where do you focus the next 60 minutes?

options.label: Hunt: pivot on the service account across all auth logs; check whether any backup repositories were touched.
options.consequence: You find that the actor reached the Veeam server at 01:55 but failed to delete backups (MFA on the Veeam admin role held). You can recover.

options.label: Drafting: write the customer-impact statement so it is ready for 06:30.
options.consequence: You have a polished press release at 04:30 but you have not validated whether backups survived. Recovery is now blocked on incomplete information.

options.label: Pay: explore quietly whether the bank's cyber-insurance broker can negotiate with the actor.
options.consequence: OFAC sanction risk on a known Russian-affiliated group. The CISO vetoes the conversation. You have lost an hour and surfaced a governance problem.

scenes.narrative: It is 06:15. Wire-transfer staff are walking in to find the office cordoned off. The COO is calling on the bridge. You still do not have a clean scope. The CISO is now joining and is unhappy.

decision.prompt: What do you tell the COO?

options.label: The truth, structured: scope unclear, wire transfers paused, NYDFS notification will be filed within the 72-hour window, an external IR firm is being engaged now.
options.consequence: The COO is angry but informed. He clears the budget for the IR firm and pauses wires until you give the all-clear.

options.label: Reassure: tell him this is contained and he should proceed with normal operations.
options.consequence: Wire transfers proceed on a compromised network for 90 minutes. Two ACH batches go through suspicious approval flows. The post-incident review is brutal.

scenes.narrative: By 08:00 the technical situation is stable. Now the regulatory clock is loud. NYDFS requires notification of a cybersecurity event 'as promptly as possible but in no event later than 72 hours' (23 NYCRR 500.17(a)). The bank is also a member of the FS-ISAC.

options.label: File the NYDFS Section 500.17(a) notification today with the facts you have, even though scope is still being refined. Share IOCs with FS-ISAC.
options.consequence: You file at 14:30. NYDFS acknowledges within an hour. FS-ISAC distributes the IOCs and two member banks reply that they have seen the same C2 IP in the last 24 hours.

options.label: Wait until you have a complete forensic picture before filing. Push to file at hour 71.
options.consequence: You are inside the legal window but the regulator will note the timing. The auditor will ask why a bank with an MSSP and an EDR took 71 hours to file what was knowable at hour 8.

scenes.narrative: It is now Wednesday 10:00. The IR firm is on site. Backups are intact. The infected hosts are being rebuilt from gold images. Customer-facing services have been degraded for 28 hours.

options.label: Restore the file server from yesterday's backup, validate integrity, then rotate every credential that touched the affected hosts before reopening wire transfers.
options.consequence: Wire transfers reopen Thursday 09:00. Recovery is clean. The post-incident report will note disciplined sequencing as the reason re-infection did not occur.

options.label: Restore everything from backup in parallel and reopen wire transfers as soon as the file server is back.
options.consequence: You reopen at 14:00 Wednesday. By 16:30 a re-infection alert fires from a host whose service-account credential was not rotated. You are back at scene 02.
